chunks.text: This is Egypt, about one million square kilometers.
Most of what you see is desert.
Now look at this one thin green line.
That is the Nile.
Nearly all of Egypt's people live along it, or in the Delta at its end.
Why here, and almost nowhere else?
Most Egyptians live in the Delta, or in the narrow valley south of Cairo.
Together, the valley and Delta are about four percent of Egypt's land.
Recent estimates, including NASA's, put about ninety-seven percent of its people there.
Sources differ on the exact shares, but a small part of the map holds almost everyone.
In the nineteen nineties, density in the valley and Delta was around fifteen hundred people per square kilometer.
In the rest of the country, it was a tiny fraction of that.
Move out over the desert, and the reason starts to show.
By the FAO's estimate, almost no rain falls here.
The north coast gets the most.
So Egypt leans on one river.
The FAO calls the Nile the main source of water for Egypt.
That river once brought more than water.
Its great flood usually came through Egypt and spread fertile mud over the fields beside it.
But follow the river south, far beyond Egypt's border.
Here are the highlands of Ethiopia.
By a common estimate, around eighty-six percent of the Nile's flow starts in Ethiopia.
The exact share depends on which rivers are counted.
The Blue Nile alone carries more than half of the water that reaches Egypt.
The White Nile and the Atbara bring the rest.
So most of Egypt's river starts in another country.
Now come back to Aswan.
Work on the High Dam began in nineteen sixty.
It was completed in nineteen seventy.
Behind it lies Lake Nasser.
One account says the dam brought the Nile's devastating floods to an end.
An older study says most of the river's sediment now stays in the lake.
The FAO links the dam to less silt downstream and to more fertilizer.
By our reasoning, if fertile mud were the whole answer, this strip should have lost its people.
It did not.
NASA's figure of roughly ninety-seven percent was published in twenty twelve, decades after the dam.
Our reading is that water explains more of this map than mud does.
So why does almost all of Egypt live along the Nile?
Our answer is that the valley and Delta are the one large part of this country with reliable water.
The rest is mostly desert, with very little rain.
The river brings its water from far to the south, mostly from Ethiopia.
By recent estimates, about four percent of the land holds about ninety-seven percent of the people.
Look at that green line once more.
Egypt's map of people follows water that mostly starts in another country.
